subject: Computer Science

statusNote: The code 1CP2 is confirmed by Pearson's own sample assessment materials and getting started guide. Paper structure, marks and the six topics were confirmed on Pearson-hosted documents. The section-level reference list (1.1.1 to 6.6.3), command words and AO weightings were read from a copy of the specification hosted on a school website (Issue 1, January 2020), because the Pearson specification PDF address could not be opened. tiers: None. One untiered paper set for all students, graded 9 to 1 on the total mark.

assessment.title: Principles of Computer Science
assessment.content: Topics 1 to 5: Computational thinking, Data, Computers, Networks, Issues and impact
assessment.format: Written paper, no calculator. Five compulsory questions, one per topic; multiple-choice, short, medium and extended open-response, tabular and diagrammatic questions.

assessment.title: Application of Computational Thinking
assessment.format: On-screen practical exam in Python 3, no internet access. Six compulsory programming tasks of increasing difficulty; the last requires a program written from scratch.

nonExam: No coursework or programming project. Centres must submit a Practical Programming Statement (completed by a senior leader) by 31 May of the exam year, confirming students had reasonable opportunity to design, write, test and refine Python programs. Programming language: Python 3, with the Pearson Programming Language Subset (PLS) supplied to students in the exam. Level 2 maths and computer-related maths are assessed in both papers.

aos.desc: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the key concepts and principles of computer science.
Apply knowledge and understanding of computer science to solve problems and write programs.
Analyse problems, then design, program, evaluate and refine solutions.

units.title: Computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction and subprograms
points: Explain how decomposition and abstraction help model and solve problems (1.1.1).
Explain the benefits of using subprograms (1.1.2).

units.title: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
points: Follow and write algorithms with sequence, selection, repetition and iteration over data structures (1.2.1).
Use variables, constants, strings, records and one- and two-dimensional arrays (1.2.2).
Use arithmetic, relational and logical operators (1.2.3).
Work out outputs and variable values using trace tables (1.2.4).
Identify syntax, logic and runtime errors and correct logic errors (1.2.5).
Explain how bubble sort, merge sort, linear search and binary search work (1.2.6).
Judge fitness for purpose and efficiency using test data (1.2.7).

units.title: Computational thinking: logic and truth tables
points: Complete and interpret truth tables using AND, OR and NOT, with up to three inputs (1.3.1).
Write and read logic expressions and relate them to program conditions (1.3.1).

units.title: Data: binary and number representation
points: Binary represents data and instructions; count the states available for a given number of bits (2.1.1).
Represent unsigned integers and signed integers using two's complement (2.1.2).
Convert between denary and 8-bit binary: 0 to 255, and -128 to +127 (2.1.3).
Add positive binary numbers and apply logical and arithmetic shifts (2.1.4).
Explain overflow when a result exceeds the available bits (2.1.5).
Explain why hexadecimal is used and convert between hex and binary (2.1.6).

units.title: Data: representing text, images and sound
points: Represent characters using 7-bit ASCII (2.2.1).
Describe bitmap images using pixels, resolution and colour depth (2.2.2).
Describe sound sampling using amplitude, sample rate, bit depth and sample interval (2.2.3).
Explain the limits of binary representation when the number of bits is fixed (2.2.4).

units.title: Data: storage units and compression
points: Use binary storage units from bit to tebibyte; calculate file sizes and capacities (2.3.1).
Explain why compression is needed and compare lossless and lossy methods (2.3.2).

units.title: Computers: architecture, memory and storage
points: Describe the von Neumann stored-program concept, RAM, CPU components, clock, buses and the fetch-decode-execute cycle (3.1.1).
Explain how magnetic, optical and solid-state secondary storage store data (3.1.2).
Describe embedded systems and their uses (3.1.3).

units.title: Computers: operating systems, utilities and robust software
points: Describe operating system functions: file, process, peripheral and user management (3.2.1).
Describe utility software: repair, backup, compression, defragmentation and anti-malware (3.2.2).
Explain robust software and finding vulnerabilities through audit trails and code reviews (3.2.3).

units.title: Computers: programming languages and translators
points: Compare the characteristics and purposes of low-level and high-level languages (3.3.1).
Explain how interpreters and compilers translate high-level code differently (3.3.2).

units.title: Networks: types, protocols and connections
points: Give reasons for connecting computers in networks (4.1.1).
Distinguish LAN and WAN (4.1.2).
Describe internet structure, including IP addressing and routers (4.1.3).
Explain how wired and wireless connections affect speed, range, latency and bandwidth (4.1.4).
Calculate transmission time, rate and file size from network speed in bits per second (4.1.5).
Describe protocols: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, POP3, SMTP and IMAP (4.1.6).
Describe the four-layer TCP/IP model (4.1.7).
Compare bus, star and mesh topologies (4.1.8).

units.title: Networks: network security
points: Identify network vulnerabilities through penetration testing and ethical hacking (4.2.1).
Explain protections: access control, physical security and firewalls (4.2.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: environmental effects
points: Discuss environmental impacts of computing: energy use, manufacture, replacement cycles and disposal (5.1.1).
Weigh the environmental costs of devices against their benefits when giving a reasoned view (5.1.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: ethical, legal and ownership issues
points: Discuss ethics and law of personal data: privacy, consent, ownership, misuse and data protection (5.2.1).
Discuss AI, machine learning and robotics: accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and liability (5.2.2).
Explain intellectual property: copyright, patents, trademarks and licensing (5.2.3).

units.title: Issues and impact: cybersecurity
points: Describe malware types, technical vulnerabilities and social engineering (5.3.1).
Explain protection methods: anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery (5.3.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: designing, reading and refining programs
points: Use decomposition and abstraction to solve problems (6.1.1).
Read, write, analyse and refine high-level programs (6.1.2).
Convert flowcharts and pseudocode into programs (6.1.3).
Write readable code: layout, indentation, comments, meaningful names and whitespace (6.1.4).
Find and correct logic, syntax and runtime errors (6.1.5).
Evaluate fitness for purpose and efficiency using test data (6.1.6).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: program structure and control
points: Identify the structural components of a program (6.2.1).
Use sequence, selection, repetition and iteration, each with a single entry and exit point (6.2.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: data types, variables and strings
points: Use primitive types (integer, real, Boolean, character) and one- and two-dimensional structures (6.3.1).
Use variables and constants (6.3.2).
Manipulate strings: length, position, substrings and case conversion (6.3.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: input, files, validation and authentication
points: Accept and respond to user input (6.4.1).
Read from and write to CSV text files (6.4.2).
Apply validation: length, presence, range and pattern checks (6.4.3).
Apply authentication: ID and password, and lookup (6.4.4).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: operators
points: Use arithmetic operators, including modulus, integer division and exponentiation (6.5.1).
Use relational operators (6.5.2).
Use logical operators AND, OR and NOT (6.5.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: subprograms and scope
points: Use built-in, library and user-defined subprograms (6.6.1).
Know that functions return values and procedures do not (6.6.2).
Use global and local variables appropriately (6.6.3).

commandWords.meaning: Change, add, delete or rearrange code (Paper 1 and Paper 2).
Create or manipulate an algorithm or program in the required notation or language.
Give a numerical answer with working and units.
Fill in a table, diagram or algorithm.
Create an artefact such as a truth table using the subject's notation.
Change from one representation to another, for example denary to binary.
Recall or select a fact, meaning or term.
Give an account with developed points.
Justify or exemplify a point with reasoning.
Consider all sides of an issue and reach a reasoned view (6 marks).
Produce a diagram, labelled where needed.

skills: Writing, tracing and debugging Python 3 programs under timed, on-screen conditions with no internet.
Converting between flowcharts, pseudocode and code.
Number conversions and calculations: denary, binary, hexadecimal, file sizes and transmission times.
Building truth tables and logic expressions up to three inputs.
Extended written discussion of ethical, legal, environmental and security issues (6-mark questions).
Level 2 mathematics used in both papers, for example powers of 2, ratios and units.

prerequisites.from: KS3 programming in a text-based language such as Python (selection, iteration, variables)
KS3 algorithms: decomposition, flowcharts, sorting and searching
KS3 representation of text, images and sound
KS3 hardware, software and how programs run
KS3 digital literacy: online safety, security and responsible use
KS3 functions and procedures in programming

links.topic: Powers of 2, indices and standard form
links.how: Maths supplies indices and place value; Computing applies them to bit patterns, hexadecimal and storage units.
Maths supplies unit conversion and rates; Computing applies them to file sizes and transmission times (4.1.5).
Maths supplies substitution and operator precedence; Computing applies them in arithmetic, modulus and exponentiation.
Maths defines sequences and iterative formulae; Computing expresses them as loops and traces them.

links.topic: Sets, Venn diagrams and probability logic
links.how: Maths uses AND, OR and NOT in set and Venn work; Computing uses them in truth tables and conditions.

links.topic: Electrical circuits, logic and sound waves
links.how: Physics explains waves and signals; Computing explains how sound is sampled and stored in binary.

links.topic: Data logging, sensors and embedded control
links.how: Science collects data with sensors; Computing explains embedded systems and how programs process the readings.
Geography studies resource use and waste; Computing examines energy use and e-waste from devices and data centres.

links.topic: Privacy, data protection and online safety
links.how: PSHE covers rights and responsible behaviour; Computing covers the legal and ethical use of personal data and AI.
Design and Technology designs products; Computing explains the embedded processors that control them.
